title: Coverage is not enough
summary: A suite with 100% line coverage that catches half the bugs, what a mutant is, how a mutation score is computed, and strengthening weak tests until every mutant dies.

steps.title: Every line ran. Half the bugs survived.
body: This loyalty discount has tests that execute every line, so its coverage is 100%. A mutation testing tool then planted six small bugs, one at a time, and ran the tests against each. Three bugs **survived**: every test still passed.

A **mutant** is a copy of your code with one small change, the kind of slip a person makes: `>=` becomes `>`, `&&` becomes `||`, a string becomes empty, a statement disappears. If a test fails, the mutant is **killed**. If all tests pass, it **survived**, and you have found behaviour that no test checks.
mutation score = (killed + timeout) / (killed + timeout + survived + no coverage)
Here: 3 killed out of 6, so 50%, with 100% coverage. Pick the marks in the report to see each mutant.

code: public static decimal Discount(string tier, decimal total)

steps.prompt: Which statement about coverage and mutation testing is true?
options: Coverage shows which code ran during the tests; a mutation score shows how much of that code's behaviour the tests would notice changing
100% coverage means a mutation score of 100%
Mutation testing replaces the need for coverage reports
A survived mutant always means there is a bug in the code
steps.explain: Coverage is necessary (a line no test runs cannot be checked), not sufficient. A survivor means *no test checks that behaviour*. Usually that is a missing test; sometimes the mutant is equivalent (next lesson).

steps.prompt: Each mutant from a run against a suite. Killed or survived?
items: `>=` became `>`; one test checks the exact boundary value
a `return` was removed; a test asserts on the returned list
`"EUR"` became `""`; no test looks at the currency
`&&` became `||`; a test has one condition true and the other false
a log call was removed; no test checks the log
steps.explain: A mutant dies only when some test both runs the changed code and asserts on something it changes. The last one is fine to leave: logging is rarely worth a test.

steps.title: Kill the survivors
prompt: These tests give `Loyalty.Discount` 100% coverage and a 50% mutation score (the starter). The rules:
- gold: 10% off orders of **100 or more**, 5% below that;
- silver: 5% off orders of 100 or more, nothing below;
- the discount is rounded to the cent (half up) and is **never more than 20.00**.
public static decimal Discount(string tier, decimal total)
Strengthen `LoyaltyTests` (keep or replace the starter tests) until all **seven** planted bugs die.
solution: public static TheoryData<string, decimal, decimal> Cases => new()
public void Discount_by_tier_and_total(string tier, decimal total, decimal expected)

target: public static decimal Discount(string tier, decimal total)

mutants.name: gold small orders get 10%
mutants.hint: Assert the exact discount of a small gold order, not just that it is positive.

forbid.message: No "is positive" asserts: assert exact amounts

hints: Survivors live on the boundaries (exactly 100 for each tier) and at the cap (an order where 10% is over 20.00).
`> 0` is true for both 5% and 10%: assert the exact amount (99.99 gold is 5.00, 100 gold is 10.00).
`decimal` cannot be an `[InlineData]` argument: use `TheoryData<string, decimal, decimal>` with `[MemberData]`.
steps.explain: Every test you added sits on a rule's edge or asserts an exact value. That is what mutation testing teaches in one sentence: assertions must be precise enough that a small change in the code changes the outcome.
